# Education in Greece
Education in Greece is structured into three main formal stages: preschool, primary, and secondary education, followed by tertiary (higher) education. Preschool education is compulsory for two years, covering ages 4 to 6, with the first year as pre-kindergarten and the second as kindergarten. English is introduced early from preschool and forms part of the core curriculum. Primary education (Dimotiko) is compulsory, lasting six years for children aged approximately 6 to 12, with the school year running from September 11 to June 15. Early grades focus on descriptive assessments, transitioning to graded evaluations by year 3, culminating in the "Apolytirio Dimotikou" certificate that allows automatic progression to lower secondary education.
Secondary education is divided into compulsory lower secondary education (Gymnasium) for students aged 12 to 15 and non-compulsory upper secondary education (Lyceum) lasting three years for ages 15 to 18. The Gymnasium culminates in the "Apolytirio Gymnasium" certificate, which qualifies students for upper secondary schooling. Lyceum students receive the "Apolytirio Lykeiou" diploma upon graduation, enabling access to higher education through nationally standardized Pan-Hellenic Examinations. Various types of Gymnasium and Lyceum schools exist, including Model, Experimental, Music, Art, Vocational, and Special types, some requiring entrance exams or specialization. Vocational education is provided through Vocational Lyceums (EPAL), offering dual diplomas in both general and vocational subjects, with pathways to higher education and apprenticeships.
Higher education in Greece is delivered by public and increasingly private institutions, including universities and specialist academies. Public higher education is largely tuition-free, with some postgraduate programs and private institutions charging fees. Greek universities offer programs in both Greek and English and are regulated by the National (Hellenic) Authority for Higher Education (HAHE). The education system also includes non-formal education initiatives like online courses and lifelong learning centers. Formal qualifications in Greece are aligned within the 8-level Hellenic Qualification Framework (HQF), harmonized with European standards.
While the Greek education system is comprehensive, it faces challenges including public sector corruption, incidents of school violence and bullying, and past use of corporal punishment, which was banned by 2005. Financial and administrative issues affect certain vocational and post-secondary institutions. Efforts continue to modernize education delivery, expand vocational training quality, and integrate values such as active citizenship and sustainable development into curricula.
